questions.prompt: If the gradient is Lipschitz with constant \(L\), the descent lemma says
options: \(f(y) \le f(x) + \nabla f(x)^T(y - x) + (L/2)\lVert y - x\rVert^2\)
\(f(y) \ge f(x) + \nabla f(x)^T(y - x) + (L/2)\lVert y - x\rVert^2\)
\(f(y) \le f(x) + (L/2)\lVert y - x\rVert^2\), with no linear term
\(f(y) = f(x)\) for every \(y\)
questions.explanation: The lemma is an upper bound: the linear model plus a quadratic penalty of coefficient \(L/2\). The reversed inequality is not what Lipschitz continuity of the gradient gives. Dropping the linear term is valid only when the gradient vanishes. The bound does not force \(f\) to be constant.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(t) = 2 t^2\), which has Lipschitz constant \(L = 4\) for its derivative. At \(t = 1\), \(f = 2\) and \(f' = 4\). What upper bound does the descent lemma give at \(t = 2\)?
questions.explanation: The step is \(d = 1\). The bound is \(2 + 4 \cdot 1 + (4/2) \cdot 1^2 = 2 + 4 + 2 = 8\). The true value \(f(2) = 8\) meets the bound, which is what a sharp constant does for this quadratic. Reporting \(6\) forgets the quadratic term. Reporting \(2\) is the old value. Reporting \(4\) is the derivative.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: The descent lemma needs a Lipschitz gradient. It does not need
options: differentiability of \(f\)
a finite constant \(L\)
the points to be joined by a segment
convexity of \(f\)
questions.explanation: The proof integrates the gradient along the segment and bounds the change in the gradient by \(L\). Convexity is a different hypothesis and produces a lower bound, not this upper bound. Differentiability is already part of having a gradient. The constant has to be finite, and the segment is the path the integral uses.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order of the proof of the descent lemma. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The integral representation comes first. Splitting off the known gradient leaves the remainder that the Lipschitz condition can bound. The factor \(t\) in that bound is what integrates to \(1/2\). Integrating before the bound exists does not yet produce \(L/2\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 180" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a segment</title><line x1="28" y1="150" x2="256" y2="150"/><polygon points="256,150 249.6,152.7 249.6,147.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="40" y1="164" x2="40" y2="20"/><polygon points="40,20 42.7,26.4 37.3,26.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="166" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="48" y="16" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="36" y1="132" x2="244" y2="36" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="70" y1="112" x2="190" y2="52" stroke-width="2.4"/><circle cx="70" cy="112" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/><circle cx="190" cy="52" r="2.6" fill="currentColor"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A solid segment joins two marked points on a dashed line.
steps: Write \(f(y) - f(x)\) as the integral of \(\nabla f(x + t(y - x))^T(y - x)\) for \(t\) from \(0\) to \(1\).
Split the integrand into \(\nabla f(x)^T(y - x)\) plus the change in the gradient.
Bound that change by \(L t \lVert y - x\rVert^2\), using the Lipschitz condition.
Integrate the bound in \(t\) from \(0\) to \(1\) to produce the term \((L/2)\lVert y - x\rVert^2\).

questions.prompt: Let \(f(t) = t^2\), whose derivative has sharp Lipschitz constant \(L = 2\). Which statements are true?
options: With \(L = 2\), the descent-lemma upper bound equals \(f(y)\) for every \(y\).
Replacing \(L\) by \(1\) makes the bound fail for some \(y\).
Replacing \(L\) by \(4\) keeps a valid upper bound.
The bound does not use the gradient.
\(L = 0\) is a valid Lipschitz constant of this derivative.
questions.explanation:
For a quadratic whose Hessian equals \(L\), the descent lemma is an equality.
• With \(L = 2\), the upper bound simplifies to \(y^2\), which is \(f(y)\).
• At \(x = 1\) and \(y = 3\), the bound with \(L = 1\) is \(1 + 2 \cdot 2 + (1/2) \cdot 4 = 7\), while \(f(3) = 9\).
• Any larger constant, including \(4\), still dominates the Hessian norm.
• The linear term is the gradient. Dropping it is a different expression.
• \(L = 0\) would require a constant derivative, and \(f'(t) = 2t\) is not constant.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 230" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>nested contours</title><line x1="28" y1="118" x2="272" y2="118"/><polygon points="272,118 265.6,120.7 265.6,115.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="204" x2="150" y2="26"/><polygon points="150,26 152.7,32.4 147.3,32.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="266" y="134" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="158" y="30" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><ellipse cx="150" cy="118" rx="40" ry="24"/><ellipse cx="150" cy="118" rx="72" ry="44"/><ellipse cx="150" cy="118" rx="104" ry="62"/></svg>

questions.prompt: The value \(f(x)\) is \(f_0\), the directional derivative along a step of length \(h\) is \(g \cdot h\) with slope \(g\), and the Lipschitz constant is \(\mathrm{ell}\). The descent-lemma upper bound equals
questions.explanation: The bound is the current value, plus the linear term \(g h\), plus \((\mathrm{ell}/2) h^2\). All four names appear. Using \(\mathrm{ell}\, h^2\) without the one-half doubles the quadratic term. Dropping \(g h\) erases the slope. Subtracting the quadratic term produces a lower model, which is not the lemma.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: A note records the descent lemma. Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The linear term is the gradient at \(x\). The Lipschitz condition contributes a factor \(t\) inside the integral, and \(\int_0^1 t\, dt = 1/2\). The false step drops that one-half and writes \(L\) in front of the squared distance. The integral of a constant \(L\), with no factor \(t\), is what would have produced a bare \(L\).

questions.figure_alt: A solid segment joins two marked points on a dashed line.
steps: The first-order term in the upper bound is \(\nabla f(x)^T(y - x)\).
Along the segment, the gradient changes by at most \(L t \lVert y - x\rVert\) in norm.
Integrating that bound from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 1\) produces the coefficient \(L/2\).
The descent lemma therefore bounds the remainder by \(L \lVert y - x\rVert^2\), with no factor \(1/2\).
reasons: The integral of \(t\) from 0 to 1 is \(1/2\). The coefficient is \(L/2\), not \(L\).
The linear term is not the gradient inner product.
The Lipschitz bound on the gradient change does not grow with \(t\).

questions.prompt: Continue \(f(t) = 2 t^2\) with \(L = 4\). At \(t = 2\), \(f = 8\) and \(f' = 8\). What upper bound does the descent lemma give at \(t = 3\)?
questions.explanation: The step is \(d = 1\). The bound is \(8 + 8 \cdot 1 + (4/2) \cdot 1 = 18\). The true value \(f(3) = 18\) matches it. Reporting \(16\) forgets the quadratic term. Reporting \(8\) is the old value. Reporting \(26\) uses the derivative \(16\) of a different function, \(4 t^2\), in place of \(f' = 8\).
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Compared with the tangent lower bound that convexity gives, the descent lemma
options: requires the Hessian to be indefinite
does not involve the gradient
runs the other way: it is an upper bound, and the extra term is quadratic
is the same inequality
questions.explanation: Convexity says \(f(y) \ge f(x) + \nabla f(x)^T(y - x)\). The descent lemma says \(f(y)\) is at most that same linear expression plus \((L/2)\lVert y - x\rVert^2\). One is a lower bound and the other is an upper bound. An indefinite Hessian is not the hypothesis. The gradient is the linear term in both.

questions.prompt: A gradient step \(y = x - t \nabla f(x)\) plugged into the descent lemma produces a guaranteed decrease when
options: the gradient is zero
\(t\) equals the condition number
questions.explanation: Substitute \(y - x = -t \nabla f\). The upper bound becomes \(f(x) - t(1 - L t/2)\lVert\nabla f\rVert^2\). The coefficient \(1 - L t/2\) is positive precisely when \(t < 2/L\). A longer step can make the upper bound increase. The condition number is not this threshold. A zero gradient makes the decrease zero, which is not the interesting case.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Now let \(f(t) = t^2\) with \(L = 2\). At \(t = 2\), \(f = 4\) and \(f' = 4\). What upper bound does the descent lemma give at \(t = 5\)?
questions.explanation: The step is \(d = 3\). The bound is \(4 + 4 \cdot 3 + (2/2) \cdot 9 = 4 + 12 + 9 = 25\). The true value \(f(5) = 25\) meets it. Reporting \(16\) stops after the linear term. Reporting \(13\) adds the step length to the old value. Reporting \(4\) is the old value.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: A conditional-gradient step minimizes a linear model over a set and then uses the descent lemma to
options: choose a step length that keeps a guaranteed decrease of the smooth objective
prove the feasible set is a simplex
remove the Lipschitz constant from the argument
replace the objective by a constraint
questions.explanation: The linear minimization produces a direction. The descent lemma turns a step along that direction into an upper bound on the new value, and a standard step-length rule makes the bound decrease. The geometry of the feasible set is a separate hypothesis. The Lipschitz constant stays in the estimate. The objective is not replaced.
